holds.reason: This is a 2008 Crescent City harbor and approach survey. Its descriptive report identifies significant channel shoaling, numerous uncharted rocks along the southern offshore edge, and incomplete full-bottom coverage of the approach. The five eligible 4 m screen cells overlapping a predicted-hard polygon (about 80 square meters) cannot establish a natural fishing reef or a safe approach. Keep the survey for harbor-source review; do not promote it to a fishing target without a current chart, site-specific original-cell review and separate substrate evidence.

The 2009 Stil Well Point–Greenwood Cove survey contains fine measured depth and historical rocky-camera overlap, but its original report identifies five dangers to navigation, charted rocks/islets needing correction, and holidays where least depths were not established. The NOAA NBS sample has 60 locally qualified rocky-camera windows, yet only 18 also pass the strict 25 m original-BAG native-grid and depth screen; 37 are held at original fine-grid edges. Do not promote a Fort Bragg–Point Arena target until hazards are reconciled with the current ENC, exact source footprints and position uncertainty are reviewed, and local species/method rules and access pass separately.

The 2009 Big White Rock–Abalone Point survey contributes measured cells to another North Mendocino NOAA NBS test tile. Of 35 tile-qualified historical rocky-camera windows, only seven pass the exact original 222 MB BAG fine-grid/depth/uncertainty neighborhood screen; 25 are held at original fine-grid edges and three fail original cell qualification. Its report identifies four dangers to navigation and chart contour and shoal discrepancies, including a 10-fathom contour displaced by as much as 400 m in an older chart comparison. Keep the survey as a source lead, not a fishing target, until the current ENC, historical hazards, exact substrate and MPA footprints, access and Mendocino rules are reviewed.

The 2008–2009 Point Delgada survey is the measured contributor behind a North Mendocino NOAA NBS test tile with 46 historically rocky camera windows passing the tile's 25 m screen, but only three also pass the original 242 MB BAG's fine-grid/depth/uncertainty neighborhood screen; 43 are held near original fine-grid edges. Its final descriptive report identifies seven dangers to navigation, two rocks of unknown depth over shallow shoal holidays, charted-islet corrections and dynamic sediment bottom. Withhold the survey from fishing-target promotion until current ENC hazards, exact substrate and MPA footprints, access and Mendocino rules are reconciled. The tile and 2010 camera records alone do not locate a present fishable reef.

The 2017 San Miguel Passage original variable-resolution BAG has millions of native cells in the 25–200 ft/uncertainty screen, but the descriptive report identifies three danger-to-navigation soundings, chart-contour discrepancies near eastern San Miguel, a sand spit with mobile sand waves and possible coverage gaps. Do not convert native depth alone into reef targets. Reconcile exact hard substrate, all report hazards, current ENC and access/MPA/method rules first.

The 2019 Prisoners Harbor to Cavern Point original MLLW variable-resolution BAG has millions of native fine cells passing the preliminary depth and product-uncertainty screen. The report's section D.1.4 nevertheless identifies three new obstructions in the Final Feature File, despite D.1.2 saying no shoals or potentially hazardous features exist. The report also describes incomplete nearshore navigable-area coverage. Keep this survey as a depth lead, not a fishing target, until obstruction positions and current ENC are reconciled with each candidate footprint, exact hard substrate and closures are screened, and local access and fishing rules pass.

The 2019 Bowen Point to Posa Anchorage original MLLW variable-resolution BAG has millions of native fine cells passing the preliminary depth and product-uncertainty screen. The report's section D.2.9 says sea conditions and time limits prevented defining the navigable-area limit in the western half and that most mapped features there were not investigated. Keep the full survey on hold until the report's Figure 21 and feature positions are georeferenced, incomplete areas are excluded, current ENC and exact substrate are checked, and MPA, access and local fishing rules pass. A reported absence of shoals elsewhere does not resolve this coverage gap.

The 2019 eastern Santa Cruz original MLLW variable-resolution BAG has 14,160,432 native 1–4 m cells across the survey; 4,737,914 of the cells in the candidate habitat review area passed a 60–200 ft depth, 2 m planning-margin and 1 m product-uncertainty screen. A native-cell/historical-hard-substrate/closure trial generated eight research patches, one B and seven C, not public fishing targets. The survey report identifies two unresolved holidays and steep rocky nearshore features rising about six to seven meters off the bottom. Figure 16 and Figure 22 are not precise hazard masks. Withhold all eight until the gap and rock positions are georeferenced against the original grid and current ENC, individual patches clear those buffers, and local fishing rules and access are checked. The surveyed depths are not a safe route or proof of catch.

The November 2022 Santa Rosa original BAG has valid MLLW depth and product uncertainty and overlaps historical hard-substrate mapping outside current MPA/GEA snapshots. However, its two 25–200 ft candidate patches score only 19 and 8 on the uncalibrated 100-point physical habitat rubric (both C): approximately 117–125 ft, little measured relief, and no bottom samples or verified catch. Do not publish these flat patches as promising rockfish or lingcod grounds. Retain as a source lead pending stronger local substrate or catch evidence and current chart/access review.
